strengths: The paper addresses a well-defined problem of interest to researchers in GP active learning and multiobjective optimization: identifying an approximate Pareto set over a continuous design space.

Adaptive partitioning, inherited confidence regions, and the refinement-versus-evaluation rule form a useful algorithmic framework. Accommodating dependent GP outputs and studying both information gain and metric dimension offer informative perspectives.
The staged algorithm description, partition illustration, extensive appendix, and implementation link help readers understand and use the approach.
The experiments include squared-exponential and Matérn kernels, several established optimizers, ten-run hypervolume curves, and an informative comparison of runtime across depth limits.
weaknesses: Necessary: Correct the confidence calibration underlying Theorem 1. Corollary 1 defines V_h using log(h²) while allowing h = 0, and its union bound sums h^(-2) starting at zero. Thus the root parameter is undefined. Moreover, substituting the displayed u into Lemma 7 produces 2h log N, whereas V_h contains h log N. Supply valid root handling and a consistent union bound, then propagate the corrections into h_max, β, and the stated guarantees.

Necessary: Resolve gaps in the termination and dimension-bound arguments. Definition 10 excludes nodes with tied maximal lower corners, potentially making the pessimistic Pareto set empty. With two tied best boxes and one dominated box, the latter need not be discarded even when every diameter is below ε, contradicting the argument in Lemma 3. Specify tie handling. Separately, Lemma 14, equations (32) and (34), assumes that a parent's refinement inequality remains true at a later evaluation count. Because β increases, this does not follow from decreasing posterior variance. An argument using the confidence region inherited at the actual refinement time may repair this step, but the supplied proof does not establish it.

Necessary: Example 1 does not establish the claimed linear information gain or complementarity of the bounds. Its lower bound is T multiplied by a quantity involving the terminal amplitudes a_(T,j), which can approach zero under the stated assumptions. Keeping the independent peak amplitudes bounded away from zero creates infinitely many separated points in the GP metric, incompatible with the Hölder comparison on a compact design space. Provide a construction satisfying all assumptions, including an explicit admissible metric, or withdraw this example and narrow the associated claims.

Necessary: Align the experimental metrics with the formal guarantee. Section 6.1.3 measures coverage using nearest-point proximity within 2ε, whereas Definition 4 requires coordinatewise, one-sided ε-dominance. Consequently, 100% reported coverage does not establish the theorem's covering condition. Specify the distance used and evaluate the formal criterion directly. The claim that input-grid spacing below ε/10 makes the discretized front sufficiently accurate also needs an objective-variation bound or a clearly stated approximation limitation.

Necessary: Support or narrow the comparative claims and clarify the experimental protocol. The introduction claims substantial improvements over ε-PAL, but Section 6 compares against PESMO, ParEGO, and USeMO without an ε-PAL baseline. The dramatic runtime reduction uses a depth cap that sets V_h to zero and removes the stated guarantee; those results must be distinguished from guarantees for the theoretical algorithm. Report the observation-noise variance, termination evaluation counts, and ε/depth settings for Simulations II–V sufficiently clearly to assess and reproduce the comparisons.

Optional: Experiments with correlated objectives, learned kernels, and larger input dimensions would clarify practical applicability. These extensions are not prerequisites for an interesting contribution under the stated model; the unresolved correctness and evidence issues above drive the recommendation.
